notes.en: Or perhaps it is only a generalization in the first generalization, and so on: Rabbi Yishmael wants to learn from both, from the generalization and the detail and from Rav Huna’s count: from the generalization and detail he learns “anything whose smoke rises,” and from the verse he learns how many there are. For if only from the generalization, it is difficult to him: say the last “spices” are two, and so on.

messages.text: The Master said: Or perhaps it is only that the second generalization is in the same category as the first generalization, and the second detail is in the same category as the first detail. You must say that this is not the case; consequently, you cannot learn in accordance with the last version, but rather you must learn in accordance with the first version. What is the difficulty alluded to here by the baraita?
messages.lead: The Gemara clarifies the latter clause of the baraita.
messages.quote: Or perhaps it is only that the second generalization is in the same category as the first generalization

messages.text: This is what is difficult to the tanna: Let us say that the last mention of “spices” is referring to two ingredients, just as the first mention of “spices” is referring to two ingredients. The tanna then answered as we answered earlier, that if so, let the verse write: Spices, spices, stacte, and onycha, and galbanum, in that order.
And what is the meaning of the suggestion: The second detail is in the same category as the first detail?

This is what is difficult to the tanna: Since it is derived by the principle of a generalization, and a detail, and a generalization that all items similar to those specified in the verse are included, as stated earlier that spices from types of trees are derived from the mention of stacte and spices grown from the ground are derived from the mention of onycha, one might say as follows: Let them also learn from the mention of pure frankincense, which includes one aspect, i.e., that one should include an item whose scent diffuses, even though its smoke does not rise.

notes.he: והיינו דפריך או אינו אלא פרט אחרון דהיינו לבונה. בפרט ראשון מייתי נמי דדמי ליה ולמעוטי דבר [שאין] ריחו נודף ולא קוטר ועולה נאמרה לי כשאר פרטי קמאי דמייתי מאי דדמי ליה:
notes.en: And let them also learn from frankincense, and so on: this is what it challenges with “or perhaps it is only…”: the last detail, that is, frankincense, should also bring what is similar to it, as the first detail does; and the exclusion of something whose scent does [not] diffuse and whose smoke does not rise would then be stated to me, like the other, first details, from which one brings what is similar to them.

notes.he: ונילף נמי מן פרט אחרון מן לבונה זכה דנייתי אפילו הני דלית בהו אלא חד צד דומיא דלבונה דריחה נודף ולפיק חד מהנהו דקוטר ועולה ואע"פ שאינו קוטר:
notes.en: And let it also learn from the last detail, from pure frankincense, that we should bring even those that have only one aspect, like frankincense, whose scent diffuses, and let it take out one of those whose smoke rises, even though [the one brought in its place] does not rise.

messages.text: The tanna then said that this cannot be the case, as if so, let the verse write “pure frankincense” in the middle, between the two mentions of “spices,” alongside stacte, onycha, and galbanum, and then one would derive this halakha from it. Since the frankincense is mentioned after the second mention of “spices,” it is not part of the generalization, detail, and generalization.

notes.he: דכשאר פרטי מייתי ליה נכתביה במיצעי בהדי שאר פרטי קמאי והיינו דקאמר לאו:
notes.en: If so: if one brings it like the other details, let it write it in the middle, with the other, first details. And that is why it says: No.

notes.he: דילפינן מינה ניכתוב קרא ללבונה במיצעי קודם סמים בהדי אידך פרטי אלא מדכתבה לבסוף ש"מ הא אין עליך לדון בלשון כו':
notes.en: He then said: If so, that we learn from it, let the verse write frankincense in the middle, before “spices,” with the other details. Rather, since it wrote it at the end, conclude from it: you cannot learn in accordance with the language, and so on.

messages.text: If the verse were to write “pure frankincense” in the middle, there would be twelve ingredients in the incense, as that ingredient would also be included in the doubling of the second mention of “spices.”

notes.he: וקפריך ליה הש"ס הא לאו תירוצא הוא דאי כתבה ללבונה בהדי שאר פרטי בין שני הכללות הויין תרי סרי כגון סמים ב' ונטף ושחלת וחלבנה ולבונה הרי ו' וסמים כנגדן הרי י"ב ולהכי לא כתבה בהדי פרט דלא תימא י"ב בעינן ולעולם גמר מיניה:
notes.en: And the Gemara challenges it: this is no answer, for had it written frankincense with the other details between the two generalizations, there would be twelve: “spices,” two; stacte, onycha, galbanum and frankincense, that is six; and “spices” corresponding to them, that is twelve. That is why it did not write it with the detail, so that you should not say twelve are required; but in fact one does learn from it.

messages.text: If so, that frankincense is meant to be one of the details, let the verse write “pure frankincense” in the middle and “galbanum” at the end, after the second mention of “spices.” Since the verse placed frankincense at the end, one cannot derive halakhot from it as a detail.

notes.he: דנשמע מיניה די"א הן ונשמע מיניה דאפילו אינו קוטר ועולה ונכתב חלבנה לבסוף דהא השתא מיהא לאו מידי גמרינן מיניה:
notes.en: If so, let it write it in place of galbanum: so that we would learn from it that there are eleven, and we would learn from it [that one brings an item] even if [its smoke] does not rise; and let it write galbanum at the end. Now, at any rate, we learn nothing from it.

notes.he: אי משום הא לא איריא דאילו אי כתבה ללבונה במיצעי הוויין תרין עשר דאמרי' סמים בתראי שיתא כי הנך ד' דבפרט וב' בכלל אלא הכי מצית למימר א"כ דלמילף מינה אתיא לבונה ליכתבה במצעי וחלבנה לבסוף בתר סמים ולא הוויין אלא חד סר אלא מדלא כתבה במיצעי ש"מ דאין עליך לדון בלשון אחרון דמייתי אפי' דחד צד אלא בלשון ראשון מכלל ופרט מה הפרט מפורש דבר שקוטר ועולה וריחו נודף:
notes.en: If because of this, it is no proof; for had it written frankincense in the middle, there would be twelve, since we would say the last “spices” are six, like the four in the detail and the two in the generalization. Rather, you can say thus: If so, that frankincense comes to be learned from, let it write it in the middle and galbanum at the end, after “spices,” and there would be only eleven. Since it did not write it in the middle, conclude from it that you cannot learn in accordance with the last version, which brings even those with one aspect, but in accordance with the first version, from the generalization and detail: just as the detail is explicit, an item whose smoke rises and whose scent diffuses.

messages.text: This halakha can be derived from the word incense itself: What is the meaning of the term incense [ketoret]? It means an item that produces smoke [koter] and rises.

notes.he: לא צריך למילף לא ממנינא ולא מכלל ופרט אלא מן גופה מן שם דקטרת מה לשון קטרת דבר שקוטר ועולה ולא משכחת לה דקוטר ועולה אלא הנך י"א:
notes.en: Reish Lakish said: there is no need to learn it either from the count or from the generalization and detail, but from itself, from the name ketoret: what is the meaning of the term ketoret? An item whose smoke rises; and you find none whose smoke rises except these eleven.

messages.text: Any fast that does not include the participation of some of the sinners of the Jewish people is not a fast, as the smell of galbanum is foul and yet the verse lists it with the ingredients of the incense.

notes.he: שאין מפושעי ישראל שחוזרין בתשובה ומתענין אינה תענית:
notes.en: [Any fast] that does not include some of the sinners of Israel who repent and fast is not a fast.

messages.text: This is derived from here: “It is He Who builds His upper chambers in the heavens and has established His bundle on the earth” (Amos 9:6), i.e., when the people are united as a bundle, including their sinners, they are established upon the earth.

verse.he: הַבּוֹנֶה בַשָּׁמַיִם מַעֲלוֹתָו וַאֲגֻדָּתוֹ עַל־אֶרֶץ יְסָדָהּ הַקֹּרֵא לְמֵי־הַיָּם וַיִּשְׁפְּכֵם עַל־פְּנֵי הָאָרֶץ יְהֹוָה שְׁמוֹ׃ {פ}
verse.en:
Who built the chambers in heaven
And founded the vault on the earth,
Who summons the waters of the sea
And pours them over the land—
Whose name is GOD.

notes.he: משמע שכולן ביחד אז על ארץ יסדה:
notes.en: And His bundle: implies that when they are all together, then He has established it on the earth.

notes.he: כלומר כשהן באגודה אחת על הארץ הטובים והרעים ומשברים לבם וחוזרין הקב"ה יסדה העולם מתקיים בשבילן:
notes.en: From here: “And has established His bundle on the earth”: that is, when they are in one bundle on the earth, the good and the bad, and they break their hearts and return, the Holy One, Blessed be He, has established it: the world endures for their sake.

messages.text: § The mishna includes in its list of those liable to receive karet: And one who applies the anointing oil to his skin.
One who applies the anointing oil to animals or vessels is exempt, and one who applies it to gentiles or to corpses is exempt.
messages.lead: The Sages taught in a baraita:

messages.text: Granted, one is exempt in the case of animals and vessels, as it is written: “Upon the flesh of a person it shall not be applied” (Exodus 30:32), and animals and vessels are not the flesh of a person. It is also clear why one is exempt if he applies it to a corpse, as once someone has died, the body is called a corpse and not a person. But if one applies anointing oil to gentiles why is he exempt? Aren’t they included in the meaning of the term person [adam]?
messages.quote: to gentiles or to corpses is exempt

verse.he: עַל־בְּשַׂר אָדָם לֹא יִיסָךְ וּבְמַתְכֻּנְתּוֹ לֹא תַעֲשׂוּ כָּמֹהוּ קֹדֶשׁ הוּא קֹדֶשׁ יִהְיֶה לָכֶם׃
verse.en: It must not be rubbed on any person’s body, and you must not make anything like it in the same proportions; it is sacred, to be held sacred by you.

messages.text: Indeed they are not. As it is written: “And you My sheep, the sheep of My pasture, are people [adam]” (Ezekiel 34:31), from which it is derived that you, the Jewish people, are called adam, but gentiles are not called adam.

verse.he: וְאַתֵּן צֹאנִי צֹאן מַרְעִיתִי אָדָם אַתֶּם אֲנִי אֱלֹהֵיכֶם נְאֻם אֲדֹנָי יֱהֹוִה׃ {פ}
verse.en: For you—My flock, the flock that I tend—are human; and I am your God—declares the Sovereign GOD.

messages.text: But isn’t it written: “And the people [nefesh adam] were sixteen thousand” (Numbers 31:40). This indicates that gentiles are also referred to as adam.
messages.lead: The Gemara raises an objection based on a verse discussing captives taken during the war against Midian.

verse.he: וְנֶפֶשׁ אָדָם שִׁשָּׁה עָשָׂר אָלֶף וּמִכְסָם לַיהֹוָה שְׁנַיִם וּשְׁלֹשִׁים נָפֶשׁ׃
verse.en: And the number of human beings was 16,000, from which GOD’s levy was 32.

messages.text: That term serves to exclude, i.e., to distinguish between the people who were taken captive and the animals that were taken as spoils of war, which are also mentioned in that verse.
messages.lead: The Sage who was asked this said to the questioner:

notes.he: משום דכתיב בהמה בההוא עניינא דלא סגי דלא קרי להו אדם:
notes.en: To exclude animals: because animals are written in that passage, it could not avoid calling them adam.

notes.he: ונפש אדם דכתיב לאפוקי בהמה אתי כלומר דמנפש אדם הוו ששה עשר אלף מלבד הבהמות:
notes.en: That one: the “and the people [nefesh adam]” that is written comes to exclude animals; that is, of the people there were sixteen thousand, aside from the animals.

messages.text: But isn’t it written: “And should I not have pity on Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than one hundred and twenty thousand people [adam] who cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand, and also much cattle” (Jonah 4:11). The inhabitants of Nineveh were gentiles.

verse.he: וַאֲנִי לֹא אָחוּס עַל־נִינְוֵה הָעִיר הַגְּדוֹלָה אֲשֶׁר יֶשׁ־בָּהּ הַרְבֵּה מִשְׁתֵּים־עֶשְׂרֵה רִבּוֹ אָדָם אֲשֶׁר לֹא־יָדַע בֵּין־יְמִינוֹ לִשְׂמֹאלוֹ וּבְהֵמָה רַבָּה׃
verse.en: And should not I care about Nineveh, that great city, in which there are more than a hundred and twenty thousand persons who do not yet know their right hand from their left, and many animals as well!”

messages.text: That term serves to exclude them from the animals mentioned in the verse.
And if you wish, say instead a different reason why one who applies anointing oil to gentiles is exempt.

Anyone included in the obligation not to apply anointing oil to himself or others is likewise included as subject to the prohibition of: It shall not be applied, i.e., it is prohibited to apply the oil to him. And anyone not included in the obligation not to apply anointing oil to himself or others is not included as the object of: It shall not be applied. Only Jews are included in the prohibition against applying the anointing oil.
messages.lead: This is as a tanna teaches before Rabbi Elazar:

notes.he: כל שהוא עובר כשהוא סך את עצמו או אחרים שמצווה שלא יסוך משמן המשחה לזר:
notes.en: Anyone included in applying: anyone who transgresses when he applies it to himself or to others, who is commanded not to apply the anointing oil to a non-priest.

notes.he: מצווים אחרים עליו שלא לסוכו:
notes.en: Is included in “it shall not be applied”: others are commanded concerning him not to apply it to him.

notes.he: ותימה להאי לישנא בהמה וכלים נמי ליגמור מהכא ולערבינהו וליתנינהו ותרי זימני פטור פטור למה לי:
notes.en: Anyone included in applying: this is puzzling according to this version: let animals and vessels also be derived from here; then let them be combined and taught together. Why do I need “exempt … exempt” twice?

notes.he: שהוא מוזהר אם סך עצמו ישנו בבל ייסך חייב נמי האחד שסכו. ועובד כוכבים כיון דאינו מוזהר אם סך עצמו אינו בבל ייסך אינו חייב האחד שסכו הילכך לעובדי כוכבים נמי פטור:
notes.en: Anyone included in applying: anyone who is warned if he applies it to himself is included in “it shall not be applied”; the other who applied it to him is also liable. And a gentile, since he is not warned if he applies it to himself, is not included in “it shall not be applied”; the other who applied it to him is not liable. Therefore for gentiles too one is exempt.

messages.text: One who applies the anointing oil to animals or vessels, or to gentiles or on corpses, is exempt. If one applies the anointing oil to kings or to priests after they had already been anointed, Rabbi Meir deems him liable and Rabbi Yehuda deems him exempt.
messages.lead: It is taught in another baraita:

notes.he: לאחר שנמשחו:
notes.en: To kings and High Priests: after they had been anointed. [Rashi’s heading reads “High Priests.”]

notes.he: מאחר שנמשחו בחניכתן ר' מאיר מחייב ור' יהושע פוטר מפרש לקמן טעמייהו:
notes.en: To kings and to priests: after they had been anointed at their initiation, Rabbi Meir deems him liable and Rabbi Yehoshua [so the text here; the daf reads Rabbi Yehuda] deems him exempt; their reasons are explained below.

messages.text: And how much oil must one apply to his skin and be liable?
Any amount.
An olive-bulk.
But doesn’t Rabbi Yehuda say that he is entirely exempt?

notes.he: ואמאי נקיט ר' יהודה שיעור כזית והא ר' יהודה פטר מה סיכה כל שהן דמכל דהו יכול לסוך חד אבר אף נתינה דעונש נמי בכל שהוא:
notes.en: And why does Rabbi Yehuda take the measure of an olive-bulk? But Rabbi Yehuda [exempts]! [A printer’s note: it seems it should read “exempts with regard to kings and priests.”] Just as applying, and so on: just as applying is any amount, for with any amount one can apply it to one limb, so too placing, for which there is punishment, is with any amount.

messages.text: When Rabbi Yehuda deems him exempt that is with regard to applying oil to kings and priests, whereas in the case of an ordinary person Rabbi Yehuda deems him liable.
Concerning what matter do Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda disagree?
They disagree concerning this issue: Rabbi Meir holds that this halakha is based on the fact that it is written: “Upon the flesh of a person it shall not be applied” (Exodus 30:32),

verse.he: עַל־בְּשַׂר אָדָם לֹא יִיסָךְ וּבְמַתְכֻּנְתּוֹ לֹא תַעֲשׂוּ כָּמֹהוּ קֹדֶשׁ הוּא קֹדֶשׁ יִהְיֶה לָכֶם׃
verse.en: It must not be rubbed on any person’s body, and you must not make anything like it in the same proportions; it is sacred, to be held sacred by you.

messages.text: and it is written: “Or whoever places any of it upon a stranger, he shall be cut off from his people” (Exodus 30:33). The wording of the prohibition teaches with regard to the liability to receive karet: Just as the act of applying the oil to the skin prohibited by the verse refers to the application of any amount, as there is no specific measure stated in this regard, so too, the act of placing the oil mentioned with regard to karet refers to any amount.

verse.he: אִישׁ אֲשֶׁר יִרְקַח כָּמֹהוּ וַאֲשֶׁר יִתֵּן מִמֶּנּוּ עַל־זָר וְנִכְרַת מֵעַמָּיו׃ {ס}
verse.en: Anyone who compounds its like, or puts any of it on a lay person, shall be cut off from kin.

notes.he: דלא אשכחן שיעור בסיכה אף נתינה כל שהוא אף על גב דנתינה בעלמא כזית כדמפרש לקמן:
notes.en: Just as applying is any amount: for we do not find a measure for applying; so too placing is any amount, even though placing in general is an olive-bulk, as is explained below.

messages.text: And Rabbi Yehuda holds: We derive the halakha of placing [netina] that is stated here, which is upon a stranger, i.e., one upon whom there is no mitzva to place the anointing oil, from the halakha of giving [netina] in general. Just as giving in general is with the amount of an olive-bulk, so too, placing anointing oil upon a stranger is with the amount of an olive-bulk.

The principle that giving [netina] in general is with the amount of an olive-bulk is derived from the verse: “And if a man eats a sacred thing in error then he shall add a fifth part in addition to it, and shall give [venatan] to the priest the sacred item” (Leviticus 22:14). This verse is referring to an item given for eating, and the minimum amount that must be consumed for an act to be considered eating is an olive-bulk.

verse.he: וְאִישׁ כִּי־יֹאכַל קֹדֶשׁ בִּשְׁגָגָה וְיָסַף חֲמִשִׁיתוֹ עָלָיו וְנָתַן לַכֹּהֵן אֶת־הַקֹּדֶשׁ׃
verse.en: but if someone eats of a sacred donation unwittingly, the priest shall be paid for the sacred donation, adding one-fifth of its value.

notes.he: דגמרינן מנתינה דונתן לכהן את הקדש דכתיב ביה אכילה (ויקרא כ״ב:י״ד) ואיש כי יאכל קדש וכל אכילה כזית:
notes.en: Placing in general is an olive-bulk: for we learn it from the placing in “and he shall give to the priest the sacred item,” where eating is written: “And if a man eats a sacred thing” (Leviticus 22:14), and all eating is an olive-bulk.

messages.text: But with regard to the mitzva of applying the oil in order to anoint kings and priests, everyone agrees it is accomplished with any amount.
messages.lead: Rav Yosef adds:

notes.he: דלא תימא כי היכי דמחייב ר' יהודה בהדיוט בפחות מכזית ה"נ בסיכת מצוה קמ"ל דסגי בכל שהוא:
notes.en: For kings and priests, everyone agrees any amount: so that you should not say that just as Rabbi Yehuda deems one liable with an ordinary person [only from an olive-bulk and not] for less than an olive-bulk, so too with anointing for a mitzva; it teaches us that any amount suffices.

notes.he: ילפינן נתינה דעל זר מנתינה דעלמא מה נתינה דעלמא בכזית דכתיב ואיש כי יאכל קדש בשגגה ויסף חמישיתו עליו ונתן לכהן והא נתינה (דהכא) [דהתם] בכזית דיליף מאכילה דקדש דאין אכילה פחות מכזית אף נתינה דעל זר נמי בכזית אבל סיכה דמלכים וכהנים שלא בזמן חניכתן דברי הכל בכל שהוא דאין בהן נתינה דלא קרינן בהו זר גמור:
notes.en: And Rabbi Yehuda holds: we derive placing upon a stranger from placing in general. Just as placing in general is an olive-bulk, as it is written: “And if a man eats a sacred thing in error, then he shall add its fifth to it and give it to the priest,” and that placing (here) [there] is an olive-bulk, which is derived from eating sacred food, for there is no eating with less than an olive-bulk, so too placing upon a stranger is an olive-bulk. But applying to kings and priests not at the time of their initiation, everyone agrees, is with any amount, since there is no placing with them. [A printer’s note: perhaps it should read: “now they are strangers,” and we call them complete strangers.] Initially: at the time of their initiation, and so on, we do not call them complete strangers.

messages.text: With regard to what matter do Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda disagree in the case of kings and priests who had already been anointed? Rabbi Meir holds that since it is written: “Or whoever puts any of it upon a stranger,” and right now the king and priest are strangers because the mitzva to anoint them no longer applies, they are included in the prohibition.

And Rabbi Yehuda holds: For the purposes of this prohibition we require that the individual in question be a stranger from his beginning to his end, and the king and priest were initially not strangers.

notes.he: דהא נמשחו מתחלה:
notes.en: Initially they were not strangers: for they were anointed at the beginning.

notes.he: מעיקרן בשעת חניכתן לאו זרים אינהו גבי שמן המשחה:
notes.en: Initially, at the time of their initiation, they are not strangers with regard to the anointing oil.

messages.text: And Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda both follow their lines of reasoning, as it is taught in a mishna (Terumot 7:2):
Continues on 7a: the mishna in Terumot on a priest’s daughter who married an Israelite and then partook of teruma.
